newsitem.title: USA: Weekly jobless claims and help-wanted ads both decline.
newsitem.headline: Weekly jobless claims and help-wanted ads both decline.

text.p: The number of Americans filing for first-time jobless benefits fell last week to the lowest level in a month, while the volume of help-wanted advertisements declined in May, according to two key reports released Thursday.

The Labour Department reported that initial jobless claims in the week ended June 21 dropped to 332,000, down from 346,000 the week before. Wall Street economists surveyed by Reuters had expected claims of 340,000.
Meanwhile, the Conference Board, a private business group, said its U.S. help-wanted advertising index fell six points in May, declining to 81.0 vs. a revised 87.0 in April.
The index read 79.0 a year ago.
"This latest decline in job advertising is not necessarily a sign that the labour market is cooling down," Conference Board economist Ken Goldstein said.
"The index has been so fixed in a narrow range of about 85 to 90 in the last two years that this latest change may only be an abberation," he said.
Jobless claims had been climbing steadily over the course of the previous few weeks. So even with a drop in claims last week, the four-week average of claims rose to its highest level in five months.
The average, which gives economists a more reliable view of trends in the labour market, jumped to 338,750 last week from 335,250 the week before.
The latest figure was at its highest level since the week ended Jan. 25, when the average reached 339,750.
The number of people continuing to claim benefits rose by 42,000 to 2,308,000 in the week ended June 14, the latest week for which that data were available.
That was up from a revised 2,266,000 the week earlier.
The Conference Board said help-wanted advertising volume fell in all nine regions in the past three months.
The steepest declines were in the Middle Atlantic, off 20.8 percent; West North Central, off 13.0 percent; and South Atlantic, off 10.2 percent.
Goldstein said that the current high level of consumer optimism will sustain consumption increases, and raise inventory demand and industrial growth.

"A faster rise in industrial growth could feed through all regions of the country and deliver a kind of economy where consumer confidence hits peaks not seen in three decades, and unemployment rates drop to levels not seen in more than four decades," Goldstein added.
The Conference Board surveys advertising volume in 51 major newspapers across the country each month.
